terraform-auth0.wrapped_text:
Terraform for Auth0
The Auth0 provider lets Terraform
configure an Auth0 tenant through
the Auth0 Management API
([provider docs](https://github.co
m/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/b
lob/v1.63.0/docs/index.md#L9-L14))
. Auth0 maintains it under the
source address `auth0/auth0`.
Auth0 is a hosted sign-in service;
the [authentication map](../../aut
hentication/authentication.md#auth
0-auth0) explains what it does and
how OAuth works. The [Terraform
map](../terraform.md) explains
Terraform itself.

The unit is one tenant. A tenant
is one isolated Auth0 space with
its own users, applications and
settings. One provider
configuration manages exactly one
tenant, and the API cannot create
tenants, so someone creates each
tenant by hand first ([tenant doc]
(https://github.com/auth0/terrafor
m-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/docs
/resources/tenant.md#L11-L12)).
Terraform signs in to the tenant
as one machine-to-machine
application, and the scopes of
that application decide what
Terraform can read and change
([One Tenant, One Identity](#one-t
enant-one-identity-one-tenant-one-
identity)).

A tenant holds these objects:

- Applications, also called
clients: the apps that sign users
in, and the programs that call
APIs.
- APIs, also called resource
servers, with their scopes.
- Client grants, which allow a
machine-to-machine application to
call an API.
- Connections: the places where
users sign in, such as a user
database or a company directory.
- Roles, organizations, and
actions, which are small programs
that run during sign-in.
- Log streams, which send the
tenant's logs to another system.
- Tenant-wide settings, such as
branding and the sign-in pages.

The provider has three families of
resources for these objects
([Three Families of Resources](#th
ree-families-of-resources-three-fa
milies-of-resources)). The family
decides what an import ID looks
like and what a destroy does.
Three more ideas explain most
plans:

- For links between objects, a
plural resource owns the whole
list, and a singular resource adds
one item ([Plural Owns, Singular A
dds](#plural-owns-singular-adds-pl
ural-owns-singular-adds)).
- An action is a draft until it is
deployed, and it runs only when it
is bound to a flow ([Actions Have
Three States](#actions-have-three-
states-actions-have-three-states))
.
- The state holds client secrets,
action secrets and
identity-provider secrets ([State
Is a Secrets Store](#state-is-a-se
crets-store-state-is-a-secrets-sto
re)).

Now compare Aiven. Both providers
are remote controls for a service
that someone else runs. In Auth0,
however, people also change the
same tenant in its dashboard every
day, so drift is normal.

The map has four parts. Mental
Models explains the ideas above.
Reading an Auth0 Configuration
says what you will see and where
to look first. Pitfalls lists the
failures that experienced users
plan around. Good and Bad
Decisions compares the common
design choices.
terraform-auth0.wrapped_original_text:
Terraform for Auth0
The Auth0 provider lets Terraform configure an Auth0 tenant through the Auth0 Management API ([provider docs](https://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/docs/index.md#L9-L14)). Auth0 maintains it under the source address `auth0/auth0`. Auth0 is a hosted sign-in service; the [authentication map](../../authentication/authentication.md#auth0-auth0) explains what it does and how OAuth works. The [Terraform map](../terraform.md) explains Terraform itself.

The unit is one tenant. A tenant is one isolated Auth0 space with its own users, applications and settings. One provider configuration manages exactly one tenant, and the API cannot create tenants, so someone creates each tenant by hand first ([tenant doc](https://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/docs/resources/tenant.md#L11-L12)). Terraform signs in to the tenant as one machine-to-machine application, and the scopes of that application decide what Terraform can read and change ([One Tenant, One Identity](#one-tenant-one-identity-one-tenant-one-identity)).

A tenant holds these objects:

- Applications, also called clients: the apps that sign users in, and the programs that call APIs.
- APIs, also called resource servers, with their scopes.
- Client grants, which allow a machine-to-machine application to call an API.
- Connections: the places where users sign in, such as a user database or a company directory.
- Roles, organizations, and actions, which are small programs that run during sign-in.
- Log streams, which send the tenant's logs to another system.
- Tenant-wide settings, such as branding and the sign-in pages.

The provider has three families of resources for these objects ([Three Families of Resources](#three-families-of-resources-three-families-of-resources)). The family decides what an import ID looks like and what a destroy does. Three more ideas explain most plans:

- For links between objects, a plural resource owns the whole list, and a singular resource adds one item ([Plural Owns, Singular Adds](#plural-owns-singular-adds-plural-owns-singular-adds)).
- An action is a draft until it is deployed, and it runs only when it is bound to a flow ([Actions Have Three States](#actions-have-three-states-actions-have-three-states)).
- The state holds client secrets, action secrets and identity-provider secrets ([State Is a Secrets Store](#state-is-a-secrets-store-state-is-a-secrets-store)).

Now compare Aiven. Both providers are remote controls for a service that someone else runs. In Auth0, however, people also change the same tenant in its dashboard every day, so drift is normal.

The map has four parts. Mental Models explains the ideas above. Reading an Auth0 Configuration says what you will see and where to look first. Pitfalls lists the failures that experienced users plan around. Good and Bad Decisions compares the common design choices.

one-tenant-one-identity.wrapped_text:
One Tenant, One Identity
The provider signs in with a domain and the
client ID and secret of a machine-to-machine
application, or with a signed JWT, or with an
API token ([provider configuration](https://gi
thub.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v
1.63.0/docs/index.md#L48-L63)). It reads the
values from environment variables such as
`AUTH0_DOMAIN`, `AUTH0_CLIENT_ID` and
`AUTH0_CLIENT_SECRET`.

Every call uses the scopes that this
application holds on the Management API. A
missing read scope does not cause an error;
the provider just reads an empty value. For
example, `client_secret` is an empty string
unless the application has the
`read:client_keys` scope ([credentials doc](ht
tps://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth
0/blob/v1.63.0/docs/resources/client_credentia
ls.md#L182)). Connection options need the
scopes `read:connections_options` and
`update:connections_options` ([options scope](
https://auth0.com/docs/troubleshoot/product-li
fecycle/deprecations-and-migrations/migrate-co
nnection-options-scope)).

Auth0 recommends one tenant for each
environment, such as development, staging and
production ([multiple environments](https://au
th0.com/docs/get-started/auth0-overview/create
-tenants/set-up-multiple-environments)). The
IDs of objects differ from tenant to tenant,
so configurations refer to objects through
resources or data sources, never through
copied IDs.

three-families-of-resources.wrapped_text:
Three Families of Resources
| Family | Examples | Import ID | What a
destroy does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Objects | `auth0_client`,
`auth0_connection`, `auth0_action`,
`auth0_log_stream` | The Auth0 ID, such as
`con_…` or `lst_…` | Deletes the object |
| Links | `auth0_connection_client`,
`auth0_trigger_actions`, `auth0_client_grant`
| Two IDs joined by `::`, such as
`con_…::<client ID>` | Removes the link |
| Singletons | `auth0_tenant`,
`auth0_branding`, `auth0_prompt`,
`auth0_guardian` | Any random UUID | Differs
by resource |

The import formats come from the Import
section of each [resource doc](https://github.
com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/tree/v1.63.
0/docs/resources). A singleton is a setting
that exists once per tenant. Its destroy can
do nothing, delete something, or turn a
protection off; the pitfall Singletons on
Destroy lists which.

plural-owns-singular-adds.wrapped_text:
Plural Owns, Singular Adds
Many links exist in two versions:

| Link | Plural resource: owns the whole list
| Singular resource: adds one item |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apps that may use a connection |
`auth0_connection_clients` |
`auth0_connection_client` |
| Actions bound to a trigger |
`auth0_trigger_actions` |
`auth0_trigger_action` |
| Scopes of an API |
`auth0_resource_server_scopes` |
`auth0_resource_server_scope` |
| Permissions of a role |
`auth0_role_permissions` |
`auth0_role_permission` |

A plural resource writes exactly its own list
and removes everything else. A singular
resource appends one item and ignores the
rest. The provider warns not to use both for
the same parent ([connection clients](https://
github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob
/v1.63.0/docs/resources/connection_client.md#L
11-L14); [trigger actions](https://github.com/
auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/do
cs/resources/trigger_actions.md#L11-L13)).
Choose one style for each parent, across all
repos and states.

connection-options-are-one-document.wrapped_text:
Connection Options Are One Document
The `options` block of an `auth0_connection`
holds the details of a sign-in method, such as
the directory of an identity provider and its
client secret. The provider sends `options` as
one whole document. The docs warn that every
nested field must be set, or existing settings
can be lost ([connection doc](https://github.c
om/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0
/docs/resources/connection.md#L14)). So a
small change to one option rewrites them all,
with the values that Terraform knows.

actions-have-three-states.wrapped_text:
Actions Have Three States
An action is code that runs in a flow, such as
`post-login`. It has three states ([write your
first action](https://auth0.com/docs/customize
/actions/write-your-first-action)):

1. A draft. `auth0_action` saves the code, and
with the default `deploy = false` it stays a
draft.
2. A deployed version. With `deploy = true`,
the code becomes the live version.
3. Bound to a flow. Only a binding, through
`auth0_trigger_actions` or
`auth0_trigger_action`, makes the action run.

So a code change in Terraform can stay a
draft, and a deployed action can stay unused.
A bound action with `deploy = true`, however,
changes live sign-ins at the next apply.

state-is-a-secrets-store.wrapped_text:
State Is a Secrets Store
The state of an Auth0 configuration holds
several kinds of secret:

- The client secrets of applications, in
`auth0_client_credentials`.
- The `secrets` of actions, in plain text
([action doc](https://github.com/auth0/terrafo
rm-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/docs/resources/
action.md#L16-L18)).
- The client secret of an identity provider,
inside connection `options`.

Newer provider versions add write-only
arguments, such as `secrets_wo` and
`client_secret_wo`, which keep a value out of
the state. They need Terraform 1.11 or later.

auth0-what-you-will-see.wrapped_text:
What You Will See
| Resource | Auth0 object | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auth0_client` | application | `app_type`,
callback and origin lists |
| `auth0_client_credentials` | sign-in method
and secret of an application | Where the
secret goes next |
| `auth0_resource_server` | API | Its
identifier, which tokens use as the audience |
| `auth0_client_grant` | access of an
application to an API | Which scopes,
especially on the Management API |
| `auth0_connection` | sign-in method |
`strategy`, a complete `options` block, secret
sources |
| `auth0_connection_client(s)` | apps enabled
on a connection | Singular or plural, and who
else manages them |
| `auth0_action`, `auth0_trigger_action(s)` |
code in a flow, and its binding | `deploy`,
runtime, secrets, where the binding lives |
| `auth0_role`, `auth0_organization` | access
groups | Who assigns users to them |
| `auth0_log_stream` | export of tenant logs |
`type`, `filters`, the target |
| `auth0_tenant`, `auth0_branding`,
`auth0_prompt` | tenant-wide settings |
Exactly one owner per tenant |

An application of type `non_interactive` is a
machine-to-machine application. A client grant
to the Management API lets such an application
change the tenant itself, so these grants
deserve a careful look.

auth0-where-to-look-first.wrapped_text:
Where to Look First
Read an Auth0 configuration in this order:

1. `required_providers`, the lock file and the
provider block. Note the version gap to the
latest release, and where the credentials and
the tenant domain come from.
2. The backend and the environment selector.
Map each state to a tenant, and flag any
tenant that two states change.
3. The singletons. Each one needs exactly one
owner per tenant.
4. The link resources. Look for singular and
plural styles on the same parent, in this repo
and in others.
5. `auth0_action`: `deploy`, the runtime, the
secrets, and where its binding lives.
6. `auth0_connection`: the strategy, the full
`options` block and its secrets.
7. `auth0_client`, its credentials and grants:
the app type, the callback and origin lists,
and grants to the Management API.
8. The data sources and outputs: lookups by
name, and secrets that leave for other
systems.
9. The `lifecycle` blocks: each
`ignore_changes` marks a field that a person
or another state owns.
10. `auth0_log_stream`: the filters and the
target system.

auth0-plan-signals.wrapped_text:
Plan Signals
| Line in the plan | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `+` on an object that exists in the tenant |
Someone deleted it in the dashboard, or
another state deleted its link; Terraform
recreates it. |
| `~` on `options` of a connection | The whole
options document will be rewritten. |
| `~ cross_origin_auth = true -> null` in
every plan | A field with a server default
that the code does not set ([issue 1029](https
://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/i
ssues/1029)). |
| `~` on `auth0_trigger_actions` | The plural
binding will write its exact list; bindings
made elsewhere disappear. |
| `-/+ auth0_log_stream` | The stream is
replaced; a stream to AWS EventBridge gets a
new partner event source. |

mixed-trigger-bindings.wrapped_text:
Mixed Trigger Bindings
`auth0_trigger_actions` writes its exact list
of actions on every create and update, and
writes an empty list on destroy. So its
destroy unbinds every action of the flow,
including actions that another configuration
bound with `auth0_trigger_action` ([code](http
s://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/
blob/v1.63.0/internal/auth0/action/resource_tr
igger_actions.go#L76-L139)).
`auth0_trigger_action` also cannot set the
order: it appends its action at the end of the
flow ([trigger action doc](https://github.com/
auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/do
cs/resources/trigger_action.md#L10-L12)). Bind
all actions of one flow in one place.

Bind all actions of one flow in one place.

two-states-one-object.wrapped_text:
Two States, One Object
Two configurations can manage the same object
without knowing it. For example, the create of
`auth0_client_grant` adopts an existing grant
for the same application and API ([grant code]
(https://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-a
uth0/blob/v1.27.0/internal/auth0/client/resour
ce_grant.go#L70-L96)). When either
configuration destroys it, the other loses it.
A `data "auth0_client"` lookup by name returns
the first match, so a duplicate name silently
picks the wrong application ([data source code
](https://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-
auth0/blob/v1.63.0/internal/auth0/client/data_
source.go#L314-L340)).

When either configuration destroys it, the other loses it. A `data "auth0_client"` lookup by name returns the first match, so a duplicate name silently picks the wrong application ([data source code](https://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/internal/auth0/client/data_source.go#L314-L340)).

singletons-on-destroy.wrapped_text:
Singletons on Destroy
A destroy of a tenant-wide setting does
different things:

| Resource | What a destroy does |
| --- | --- |
| `auth0_tenant`, `auth0_prompt` | Nothing in
Auth0; it only leaves the state ([tenant code]
(https://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-a
uth0/blob/v1.63.0/internal/auth0/tenant/resour
ce.go#L642-L644)). |
| `auth0_branding` | Deletes the Universal
Login template ([branding code](https://github
.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63
.0/internal/auth0/branding/resource.go#L177-L1
88)). |
| `auth0_attack_protection` | Turns off
breached-password detection, brute-force
protection and IP throttling ([code](https://g
ithub.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/
v1.63.0/internal/auth0/attackprotection/resour
ce.go#L837-L879)). |
| `auth0_guardian` | Turns off all
multi-factor authentication factors ([code](ht
tps://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth
0/blob/v1.63.0/internal/auth0/guardian/resourc
e.go#L693-L709)). |

So removing a singleton from the code can
weaken the security of a production tenant.

auth0-secret-pitfalls.wrapped_text:
Secret Pitfalls
These pitfalls put secrets where they do not
belong, or lose them.

Secret Pitfalls
These pitfalls put secrets where they do not belong, or lose them.

data-sources-copy-secrets.wrapped_text:
Data Sources Copy Secrets
`data "auth0_client"` stores the client secret
of the application that it reads. `data
"auth0_connection"` stores the connection
options, including an identity provider's
secret. So every configuration that only reads
these objects also holds their secrets in its
state. Newer versions add `hide_client_secret`
to both data sources ([client data source](htt
ps://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0
/blob/v1.63.0/docs/data-sources/client.md#L31)
; [connection data source](https://github.com/
auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/do
cs/data-sources/connection.md#L31)).

empty-secret-without-scope.wrapped_text:
Empty Secret Without Scope
If Terraform's application lacks
`read:client_keys`, `client_secret` reads as
an empty string, with no error ([credentials d
oc](https://github.com/auth0/terraform-provide
r-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/docs/resources/client_cre
dentials.md#L182)). A configuration that
copies the secret into AWS Secrets Manager or
into an action secret then stores an empty
value. The plan looks clean, and the app fails
to sign in later. A `postcondition` that
checks the length of the secret catches this
at plan time.

A configuration that copies the secret into AWS Secrets Manager or into an action secret then stores an empty value. The plan looks clean, and the app fails to sign in later. A `postcondition` that checks the length of the secret catches this at plan time.

connection-options-replaced.wrapped_text:
Connection Options Replaced Whole
Because `options` is one document, an update
sends all of it. Fields that the code leaves
out are wiped, secrets included, and
`ignore_changes` inside `options` does not
prevent this ([issue 860](https://github.com/a
uth0/terraform-provider-auth0/issues/860)).
Without the options scopes, the API leaves
`options` out of its answers, and updates that
contain `options` fail ([options scope](https:
//auth0.com/docs/troubleshoot/product-lifecycl
e/deprecations-and-migrations/migrate-connecti
on-options-scope)). Write the full `options`
block, and add a precondition that the secret
inputs are not empty.

secret-rotation.wrapped_text:
Secret Rotation
Auth0 rotates a client secret in the dashboard
or through the API, and a new secret can take
up to 30 seconds to work ([rotate a client sec
ret](https://auth0.com/docs/get-started/applic
ations/rotate-client-secret)). Replacing
`auth0_client_credentials` in Terraform does
not rotate the secret ([issue 1785](https://gi
thub.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/issues
/1785)). After a rotation, each copy of the
secret, in Secrets Manager, in an action
secret or in a pipeline variable, changes only
at the next apply of the configuration that
writes it.

Change Pitfalls
These pitfalls appear during normal changes
and upgrades.

deploy-and-bind.wrapped_text:
Deploy and Bind
With the default `deploy = false`, a code
change in `auth0_action` stays a draft, and
nothing changes for users. With `deploy =
true`, the change goes live at once in every
flow that binds the action. Deleting an action
that is still bound fails with `409 Conflict`.
Unbind it in one apply, and delete it in the
next ([trigger actions doc](https://github.com
/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/d
ocs/resources/trigger_actions.md#L17-L19)).

lists-stay-unless-emptied.wrapped_text:
Lists Stay Unless Emptied
Removing a list argument, such as `callbacks`
or `allowed_origins`, from the code changes
nothing in Auth0. To clear a list, set it to
`[]` ([issue 1108](https://github.com/auth0/te
rraform-provider-auth0/issues/1108)).
`allowed_origins` also defaults to the
callback URLs ([client doc](https://github.com
/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/d
ocs/resources/client.md#L213)). So a localhost
callback left in a development list also
becomes an allowed origin.

rate-limits.wrapped_text:
Rate Limits
The Management API has rate limits per tenant
([rate limit policy](https://auth0.com/docs/tr
oubleshoot/customer-support/operational-polici
es/rate-limit-policy)). A large configuration
reads many objects in every plan, even with no
changes, and it can hit the limit ([issue 1488
](https://github.com/auth0/terraform-provider-
auth0/issues/1488)). The provider then waits
and retries, so plans get slow. Calls that
Terraform makes share the limit with the apps
that use the tenant.

The provider then waits and retries, so plans get slow. Calls that Terraform makes share the limit with the apps that use the tenant.

auth0-version-gaps.wrapped_text:
Version Gaps and Deprecations
Auth0 changes its API on a schedule, and old
provider versions fall behind it. For example,
the old way of managing the enabled clients of
a connection reached its end of life on
2026-07-13 ([deprecations](https://auth0.com/d
ocs/troubleshoot/product-lifecycle/deprecation
s-and-migrations)). Auth0 names provider
1.29.0 or later as compatible with the new
endpoints ([dedicated connection endpoints](ht
tps://auth0.com/docs/troubleshoot/product-life
cycle/deprecations-and-migrations/migrate-dedi
cated-connection-endpoints)). The same page
lists Rules and Hooks as deprecated in favor
of actions. Read the changelog before each
upgrade, and upgrade in steps.

one-tenant-per-environment.wrapped_text:
One Tenant per Environment
Auth0 recommends separate tenants for
development, staging and production ([multiple
environments](https://auth0.com/docs/get-start
ed/auth0-overview/create-tenants/set-up-multip
le-environments)). A shared tenant saves a
tenant and lets staging test the real company
directory. But then the tenant-wide settings
need guards in code, two states share objects,
a staging log stream also exports production
events, and a staging apply can change
production actions. A tenant used by
production should also carry the production
tag, because the production rate limits apply
only to such tenants (same page).

A tenant used by production should also carry the production tag, because the production rate limits apply only to such tenants (same page).

least-privilege-for-terraform.wrapped_text:
Least Privilege for Terraform's Client
The provider's quickstart authorizes all
Management API scopes for Terraform's
application ([quickstart](https://github.com/a
uth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/doc
s/guides/quickstart.md#L27-L28)). That is
easy, but it includes every delete scope. A
smaller set must still include the read scopes
that some attributes depend on, such as
`read:client_keys` and
`read:connections_options`; otherwise values
read as empty. Keep the credentials in
environment variables, not in code, and prefer
a signed JWT over a shared secret ([provider c
onfiguration](https://github.com/auth0/terrafo
rm-provider-auth0/blob/v1.63.0/docs/index.md#L
29-L41)).
least-privilege-for-terraform.wrapped_original_text:

That is easy, but it includes every delete scope. A smaller set must still include the read scopes that some attributes depend on, such as `read:client_keys` and `read:connections_options`; otherwise values read as empty. one-owner-per-parent.wrapped_text:
One Owner per Parent
Use a plural link resource when one
configuration owns the parent: it removes
strays and keeps the order of actions. Use
singular resources when several configurations
each add their own item. Never mix the two on
one parent (see Plural Owns, Singular Adds).

start-from-generated-config.wrapped_text:
Start from the Generated Config
The Auth0 CLI command `auth0 tf generate`
writes Terraform files and import blocks for
an existing tenant ([generate guide](https://g
ithub.com/auth0/terraform-provider-auth0/blob/
v1.63.0/docs/guides/generate_terraform_config.
md)). It is experimental, and it does not
export secrets. It writes plural resources
such as `auth0_trigger_actions`, so check for
singular resources on the same parents before
you merge its output.
